nodes.description: The second half of induction therapy acts on a target that is not an enzyme at all. Amphotericin B is an amphiphilic macrolactone that engages Cryptococcus neoformans membrane ergosterol directly: large extramembranous aggregates physically pull the sterol out of the bilayer, and binding ergosterol rather than the minor pore-forming fraction is what makes the drug fungicidal. Selectivity rests on a single fungal-specific feature, since polyenes bind ergosterol more avidly than the mammalian cholesterol that replaces it, and the discrimination being imperfect is why the drug carries dose-limiting nephrotoxicity and why the liposomal formulation exists. Two consequences matter for this disease specifically. Because the target is a finished membrane lipid rather than a mutable gene product, clinically significant polyene resistance in cryptococcal disease is rare, which is why a drug in use for five decades remains the induction backbone. And because the killing is physicochemical rather than replication-dependent, it clears organisms from cerebrospinal fluid at a rate that can be measured directly, which is the endpoint the single-high-dose liposomal regimen was judged on. This node is a therapeutic vulnerability rather than a step in the disease.
nodes.id: Amphotericin B Extraction of Membrane Ergosterol

nodes.description: Where cellular immunity is intact the infection stays in the lung. Where it is not, and the dominant cause is advanced HIV disease, containment fails and the organism proliferates and escapes. Cryptococcal antigenaemia marks this stage and precedes meningitis, which is what makes antigen screening in advanced HIV disease a prevention strategy rather than an early diagnosis.

nodes.description: Cryptococcus neoformans carries the cytosine permease and cytosine deaminase that import flucytosine and convert it to 5-fluorouracil, a pathway mammalian cells lack, and this is the selectivity on which the drug depends. The node is a therapeutic vulnerability rather than a step in the disease, and it is recorded here because the trial evidence identifies flucytosine specifically, not antifungal therapy in general, as the component that changes mortality.

nodes.description: Inhaled yeast cells reach the alveoli and interact first with alveolar macrophages. Phagocytosis may kill the organism, but it may equally survive or replicate inside the phagocyte, so the macrophage is both the first line of defence and, when defence fails, a niche. Outcome at this step is decided by the host's immune status rather than by the inoculum.

nodes.description: Cerebrospinal fluid outflow through the infected subarachnoid space is obstructed, raising intracranial pressure in half to two thirds of patients. The pressure is not an epiphenomenon of the infection but a treatable contributor to death, which is why repeated therapeutic lumbar puncture is standard adjunctive management and is associated with a large survival difference. Separating it from the infection node is what lets drainage and antifungal therapy be recorded as acting on different steps.
